name: Whitening powder (charcoal)
lead: Charcoal whitening powders are products of activated charcoal that users brush onto teeth with the aim of removing surface stain. They are one of several consumer whitening formats alongside strips, pens, rinses and toothpastes.

Wikipedia's tooth whitening article describes whitening toothpastes as containing more abrasives and detergents than regular ones, but its text does not cover charcoal powders specifically.[1] Dental research reviewed includes a laboratory study of a charcoal-containing toothpaste and mouthwash on stained canines.[2]
No clinical studies of charcoal powders were identified.

paras: Users apply the powder with a wet toothbrush. Proponents say charcoal binds and lifts surface stains; no clinical source reviewed confirms this.

A 2020 in vitro study stained forty human canines with coffee and compared brushing with deionised water, regular toothpaste and charcoal-containing products over a simulated 90 days for colour change and enamel surface alteration.[2]

refs.title: Effect of novel charcoal-containing whitening toothpaste and mouthwash on color change and surface morphology of enamel

card.summary: Brush-on activated charcoal powder for surface stain; only lab research exists.

quick.overview:
Charcoal whitening powder is brushed onto teeth in the hope of removing surface stain.

Only a laboratory study of a related charcoal product was identified; no human trials were found.
quick.mechanism: Proponents say the charcoal adsorbs and abrades stain from enamel. It does not bleach internal tooth colour.
quick.risks: General whitening toothpastes contain abrasives; the effect of charcoal on enamel has been examined in vitro. No clinical safety data were found.
